Electra. The name belongs not to one play, but to two—one by Sophocles, one by Euripides. Both center on the loyal daughter of Agamemnon, waiting for her brother Orestes to return so they can avenge their father's murder. But the two versions reach starkly different conclusions about what that revenge means.

In Sophocles' Electra, our heroine waits with hope and patience. When Orestes arrives in disguise, she doesn't recognize him at first—she hears he's dead and grieves bitterly. Then he reveals himself, and Electra's vindication becomes the play's emotional climax. She helps her brother kill their mother Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus. The revenge succeeds. Justice is served, and Electra's suffering finally ends.

Euripides tells a darker version of the same story. In his hands, Electra lives in wretchedness, deliberately married off to a peasant by Aegisthus to degrade her. When Orestes returns, the killing of their mother is calculated and cruel, disguised as the ritual of hospitality. And afterward, there's no vindication—only horror and remorse. Both siblings are cursed by the Furies, pursued for their crime, left traumatized rather than triumphant.

What both plays share is Electra herself. In each version, she's the center—a character of passionate conviction and unrelenting grief, unshakably loyal to her dead father even when her loyalty costs her everything. She's no supporting figure in someone else's drama. She's the conscience of the play, holding fast to duty and blood kinship.

The two Electras ask the same question in different keys: is revenge justice, or is it a cycle of violence that corrupts the avenger? Sophocles suggests redemption is possible. Euripides suggests the opposite—that some debts, once paid in blood, can never be repaid.
